According to the timetable, the last bus leaves at eleven.

Will you collect the parcel, or would you prefer delivery.
Will you collect the parcel or. Would you prefer delivery?
items.answer: Will you collect the parcel, or would you prefer delivery?

rationales.Will you collect the parcel or. Would yo: The full stop splits 'or' from the alternative it introduces.

The workshop (which lasts two hours) starts at six.
The workshop (which lasts two hours starts at six).

rationales.The workshop (which lasts two hours). St: The full stop separates the main subject from its verb.
rationales.The workshop (which lasts two hours star: The closing bracket includes the main predicate, leaving only 'The workshop' outside.

findings: Agenda/support-call reused the same so clause and did not teach a different boundary.

audit.pedagogicalValue: Checks that brackets enclose supplementary information, not the main predicate.

items.setupText: Write two complete sentences in a factual report, with no deliberate fragments.
items.taskText: Which version correctly explains why the match ended early?

The match ended early. Heavy rain made the pitch unsafe.
The match ended early. Making the pitch unsafe.
The match ended early. As heavy rain made the pitch unsafe.
items.answer: The match ended early. Heavy rain made the pitch unsafe.
items.explanation: The second sentence has its own subject and finite verb, so it independently explains the first.

rationales.The match ended early. Due to heavy rain: 'Due to heavy rain' is a reason phrase, not a complete second sentence.
rationales.The match ended early. Heavy rain made t: The second sentence has its own subject and finite verb, so it independently explains the first.
rationales.The match ended early. Making the pitch: This -ing phrase is not a complete second statement and suggests the ending made the pitch unsafe.
rationales.The match ended early. As heavy rain mad: 'As' makes the explanation dependent; it should then be attached to a main clause.

audit.pedagogicalValue: Distinguishes finite main clauses from prepositional, participial and subordinate fragments.
audit.levelReason: A familiar event and a clear causal account.
audit.similarityNote: Keeps two sentences rather than merging a fragment into the first.

items.setupText: A learner calls this a run-on because it is long: 'After breakfast, I walked to the station, bought a ticket and waited for the next train.'

The phrase 'After breakfast' needs its own verb before the next comma.
It is complete: all three actions share 'I'.
The final action needs another written subject because it follows 'and'.
items.answer: It is complete: all three actions share 'I'.
items.explanation: The coordinated actions are properly connected; sentence length does not make this a run-on.

rationales.The comma after 'station' incorrectly jo: 'Bought a ticket' shares the earlier subject and is not an independent clause being joined by a comma.
rationales.The phrase 'After breakfast' needs its o: The opening time phrase is an adjunct to the main clause; it need not be a sentence itself.
rationales.It is complete: all three actions share: The coordinated actions are properly connected; sentence length does not make this a run-on.
rationales.The final action needs another written s: The subject 'I' can be shared by the third action as well as the second.

findings: Guide original mixed past return with present filing and repeated the so template.
audit.microSkill: Sentence length versus faulty clause joining
audit.pedagogicalValue: Defines a run-on by structure rather than word count.
audit.levelReason: An accessible sequence of three past actions.
audit.similarityNote: Acceptability diagnosis of a longer correct sentence.

items.setupText: The editor requests one sentence with standard grammar, retaining the contrast and both subjects.
items.taskText: Which revision repairs 'I enjoyed the concert, my partner found it too loud'?

I enjoyed the concert my partner found it too loud.
I enjoyed the concert, but my partner found it too loud.
I enjoyed the concert, finding it too loud.
items.answer: I enjoyed the concert, but my partner found it too loud.
items.explanation: 'But' joins the clauses, preserves both people and explicitly marks the contrast.

rationales.I enjoyed the concert, my partner, found: The extra comma separates the second subject from its verb without repairing the clause join.
rationales.I enjoyed the concert my partner found i: Removing the comma fuses the clauses instead of joining them correctly.
rationales.I enjoyed the concert, finding it too lo: This removes the partner and makes the loudness judgment belong to 'I'.
rationales.I enjoyed the concert, but my partner fo: 'But' joins the clauses, preserves both people and explicitly marks the contrast.

findings: Policy returned 'in the project checklist' was a strained tail and feedback did not diagnose errors.
audit.microSkill: Meaning-preserving repair of a comma splice
audit.pedagogicalValue: Checks subject reference as well as punctuation in a repair.
audit.levelReason: Everyday contrasting opinions and straightforward coordination.
audit.similarityNote: Repair must retain two different experiencers.

items.setupText: Write a complete statement about something you have not decided.
items.taskText: Which version correctly includes the question inside the statement?
options: I haven't decided. Whether to rent or buy.
I haven't decided whether to rent or buy.
I haven't decided whether. To rent or buy.
I haven't decided whether to rent or buy?
items.answer: I haven't decided whether to rent or buy.
items.explanation: The 'whether' phrase completes 'decided'; the whole sentence states an unresolved decision.

rationales.I haven't decided whether to rent or buy: The 'whether' phrase completes 'decided'; the whole sentence states an unresolved decision.
rationales.I haven't decided. Whether to rent or bu: The second part is dependent on 'decided', so this creates a fragment.
rationales.I haven't decided whether. To rent or bu: The alternatives belong after 'whether' in the same phrase.
rationales.I haven't decided whether to rent or buy: The task asks for a statement, not an echo question about the speaker's decision.

findings: Summary/tutor-explanation ended twenty repeats of one low-level clause-joining pattern.
audit.microSkill: Infinitival whether-clause within a statement
audit.pedagogicalValue: Keeps an unresolved alternative attached to its governing verb.
audit.levelReason: A common housing decision with familiar infinitives.
audit.similarityNote: Nonfinite embedded alternative, distinct from the finite wh-report in 3409.

items.setupText: Compare: (1) 'The materials remained scarce; however, we adapted the design.' (2) 'The materials remained scarce however we adapted the design.'
items.taskText: How does the boundary distinguish the natural readings of 'however'?
options: Both use 'however' to contrast scarcity with the success of the adaptation.
The first leaves the adaptation uncertain; the second confirms that it succeeded.
The first signals contrast; the second means 'in whatever way'.
The first introduces a method; the second introduces an unexpected result.
items.answer: The first signals contrast; the second means 'in whatever way'.
items.explanation: The semicolon separates an independent contrast in the first; without that boundary, the however-clause means scarcity persisted regardless of the method.

rationales.Both use 'however' to contrast scarcity: In the second version, 'however we adapted the design' is a manner-concession clause: no adaptation method removed the scarcity.
rationales.The first signals contrast; the second m: The semicolon separates an independent contrast in the first; without that boundary, the however-clause means scarcity persisted regardless of the method.
rationales.The first leaves the adaptation uncertai: The distinction is not uncertainty versus success; neither sentence states that the adaptation solved the scarcity.
rationales.The first introduces a method; the secon: This reverses the functions: contrast belongs to the first and the manner reading to the second.

findings: Report-change/students/audit-file had no coherent contrast and repeated generic feedback.
audit.microSkill: Main-clause contrast versus subordinate manner-concession
audit.pedagogicalValue: Uses clause boundaries to distinguish two legitimate however constructions.
audit.levelReason: Requires interpreting how a polyfunctional word relates clauses.
audit.similarityNote: Two grammatical readings replace a disputed optional-comma foil.

items.setupText: Three branches are being listed, each with its city. Separate the branch entries with semicolons.
items.taskText: Which version makes the three entries clear?
options: We visited North, York, Central, Derby, and South, Bath.
We visited; North, York; Central, Derby; and South, Bath.
We visited North, York; Central, Derby; and South, Bath.
We visited North; York, Central; Derby, and South; Bath.
items.answer: We visited North, York; Central, Derby; and South, Bath.
items.explanation: Each semicolon separates a complete branch-city entry; the internal commas remain inside those entries.

rationales.We visited North, York, Central, Derby,: Commas alone blur the grouping of branch names with their cities and do not meet the requested format.
rationales.We visited; North, York; Central, Derby;: The first semicolon splits 'visited' from the list it governs.
rationales.We visited North, York; Central, Derby;: Each semicolon separates a complete branch-city entry; the internal commas remain inside those entries.
rationales.We visited North; York, Central; Derby,: These boundaries split branch names from their cities and pair the wrong elements.

findings: Schedule/policy-review original was one of twenty identical however patterns.
audit.microSkill: Semicolons separating internally punctuated list entries
audit.pedagogicalValue: Distinguishes list-item boundaries from clause boundaries.
audit.levelReason: Requires tracking two levels of grouping in a short list.
audit.similarityNote: Semicolons here do not require independent clauses.

items.setupText: The words 'as the brochure makes clear' are an interruption, not the main predicate.
items.taskText: Which version correctly marks both edges of that interruption?
options: The fee, as the brochure makes clear includes equipment hire.
The fee as, the brochure makes clear, includes equipment hire.
The fee, as the brochure makes clear. Includes equipment hire.
The fee, as the brochure makes clear, includes equipment hire.
items.answer: The fee, as the brochure makes clear, includes equipment hire.
items.explanation: Removing the comma-marked interruption leaves the complete core 'The fee includes equipment hire'.

rationales.The fee, as the brochure makes clear inc: A second comma is needed after 'clear' to close the interruption before the main verb.
rationales.The fee as, the brochure makes clear, in: The opening comma belongs before 'as', not between it and its clause.
rationales.The fee, as the brochure makes clear. In: The full stop breaks the main sentence between 'The fee' and 'includes'.
rationales.The fee, as the brochure makes clear, in: Removing the comma-marked interruption leaves the complete core 'The fee includes equipment hire'.

findings: Form-change/budget-meeting had an unsupported contrast and template feedback.
audit.microSkill: Paired commas around an interrupting clause
audit.pedagogicalValue: Keeps the main subject-predicate connection intact across inserted commentary.
audit.levelReason: A complete clause is embedded parenthetically inside another.
audit.similarityNote: Clause-length interruption rather than the B1 short example phrase.

items.setupText: The intended events are: the assistant packed, and the manager checked the receipts. Keep 'While' at the start.
items.taskText: Which punctuation prevents 'the manager' from being read as the object of 'packed'?

While the assistant, packed the manager checked the receipts.
While the assistant packed, the manager checked the receipts.
While the assistant packed the manager checked, the receipts.
items.answer: While the assistant packed, the manager checked the receipts.
items.explanation: The comma closes the time clause before the new main-clause subject 'the manager'.

rationales.While the assistant packed, the manager: The comma closes the time clause before the new main-clause subject 'the manager'.
rationales.While the assistant packed the manager,: This attaches 'the manager' to 'packed' and leaves 'checked' without its intended subject.
rationales.While the assistant, packed the manager: The comma divides the first subject from 'packed' and does not mark the clause boundary.
rationales.While the assistant packed the manager c: The comma comes after the main verb and incorrectly separates it from its object.

findings: Notice-change/manager-briefing combined unrelated events and recycled all feedback.
audit.microSkill: Boundary marking prevents a temporary object misreading
audit.pedagogicalValue: Identifies where an intransitive subordinate use ends and a new subject begins.
audit.levelReason: Requires parsing a locally ambiguous sequence, not merely finding a conjunction.
audit.similarityNote: Comma resolves a garden-path reading at a clause boundary.

items.setupText: Choose standard end punctuation for a direct polite question, not a declarative instruction.
items.taskText: Which version correctly punctuates the whole request?
options: Could you tell me whether the room has a projector?
Could you tell me whether the room has a projector.
Could you tell me? Whether the room has a projector.
Could you tell me whether? The room has a projector.
items.answer: Could you tell me whether the room has a projector?
items.explanation: The outer clause is interrogative, so the question mark belongs after its complete embedded content.

rationales.Could you tell me whether the room has a: Although the embedded whether-clause uses statement order, the whole 'Could you...' construction is a direct question here.
The outer clause is interrogative, so the question mark belongs after its complete embedded content.
rationales.Could you tell me? Whether the room has: The whether-clause is separated from 'tell me', which it completes.
rationales.Could you tell me whether? The room has: The question mark interrupts 'whether' and its clause instead of closing the whole question.

findings: Email-change/complaint-review did not justify 'however' and repeated the same grammatical options.
audit.microSkill: Outer question determines end punctuation despite embedding
audit.pedagogicalValue: Contrasts a direct request containing an embedded question with a reporting statement.
audit.levelReason: Tracks clause hierarchy in a polite enquiry.
audit.similarityNote: Opposite end-mark decision to the B1 reported-question item.

items.setupText: Keep both reasons under the verb 'explained' in one ordinary sentence.
items.taskText: Which version avoids breaking one content clause away from its governing verb?
options: She explained that demand had fallen; and that costs had risen.
She explained that demand had fallen. And that costs had risen.
She explained that demand had fallen; that costs had risen.
She explained that demand had fallen and that costs had risen.
items.answer: She explained that demand had fallen and that costs had risen.
items.explanation: 'And' joins two content clauses governed by the same reporting verb.

rationales.She explained that demand had fallen; an: The second 'that' clause is a coordinated complement, not an independent clause needing a semicolon.
rationales.She explained that demand had fallen. An: The full stop leaves the second content clause as a separate fragment.
rationales.She explained that demand had fallen and: 'And' joins two content clauses governed by the same reporting verb.
rationales.She explained that demand had fallen; th: A semicolon cannot turn this second dependent content clause into an independent statement.

findings: Chart/data-check original repeated the however sentence and had no meaningful context contrast.
audit.microSkill: Coordination inside a reporting complement
audit.pedagogicalValue: Does not treat every finite verb as the start of an independent sentence.
audit.levelReason: Two coordinated embedded clauses require hierarchical parsing.
audit.similarityNote: Boundary belongs within a complement rather than between main clauses.

items.setupText: The editor wants a complete statement, not a heading.

That the venue was too small, surprising the organisers.
That the venue was too small surprised the organisers.
That the venue was too small. Surprised the organisers.
items.answer: That the venue was too small surprised the organisers.
items.explanation: The entire that-clause is the subject of 'surprised', so the sentence is complete.

rationales.That the venue was too small for the aud: The that-clause alone states content but has no main predicate in this form.
rationales.That the venue was too small, surprising: 'Surprising' does not supply the finite main predicate needed after the subject clause.
rationales.That the venue was too small. Surprised: The full stop separates the subject clause from its main verb 'surprised'.
rationales.That the venue was too small surprised t: The entire that-clause is the subject of 'surprised', so the sentence is complete.

findings: Application/training-portal tail was unnatural and the repeated however pattern offered no new skill.
audit.microSkill: Content clause as subject of a main predicate
audit.pedagogicalValue: Recognizes that initial 'that' does not necessarily make the whole sentence a fragment.
audit.levelReason: Requires distinguishing an embedded subject clause from the main predicate.
audit.similarityNote: Finite clausal subject, beyond B1 noun-phrase and -ing subjects.

items.setupText: Use ordinary dialogue punctuation. The reporting words follow the speaker's complete question.
items.taskText: Which version correctly separates the quotation from its attribution?
options: "Have you checked the seal," the technician asked?
"Have you checked the seal." The technician asked?
"Have you checked the seal"? The technician asked.
"Have you checked the seal?" the technician asked.
items.answer: "Have you checked the seal?" the technician asked.
items.explanation: The question mark belongs to the spoken question; the following attribution continues the same reporting sentence.

rationales.\"Have you checked the seal?\" the techn: The question mark belongs to the spoken question; the following attribution continues the same reporting sentence.
rationales.\"Have you checked the seal,\" the techn: The speaker's words need their question mark inside the quotation; the attribution is not itself a question.
rationales.\"Have you checked the seal.\" The techn: The quotation is a question, not a statement, and the reporting tag should not be made a separate question.
rationales.\"Have you checked the seal\"? The techn: The question mark belongs inside because it is part of the quoted speech; the attribution should remain attached.

findings: Message original mixed past arrival and present contract signing without context and repeated boilerplate.
audit.microSkill: Question-mark boundary before a dialogue tag
audit.pedagogicalValue: Separates the punctuation of quoted speech from that of its attribution.
audit.levelReason: Requires handling a direct question inside a larger reporting sentence.
audit.similarityNote: Quoted direct speech rather than indirect questioning.

items.setupText: The film's title is 'Who Owns the City?' The editor wants one statement giving its release day, retaining the question mark in the title.

The film 'Who Owns the City?' opens. On Friday.
The film 'Who Owns the City?' opens on Friday?
items.answer: The film 'Who Owns the City?' opens on Friday.

rationales.The film 'Who Owns the City?' opens on F: The title's question mark belongs to the title; the surrounding statement continues with 'opens' and ends with its own full stop.
rationales.The film 'Who Owns the City?' Opens on F: The title's question mark does not start a new sentence, so 'opens' should not be capitalized.
rationales.The film 'Who Owns the City?' opens. On: The final time phrase becomes a fragment and no longer stays in the requested single statement.

findings: Contract/customer-update original was an unsupported however contrast with non-diagnostic feedback.
audit.microSkill: Title-internal question mark does not end the containing statement
audit.pedagogicalValue: Tracks punctuation inside a named work separately from its host sentence.
audit.levelReason: Requires distinguishing a title's form from the containing clause's function.
audit.similarityNote: Replaces a repeated colon lead-in exercise with nested title punctuation.

items.setupText: Compare: (1) 'If the card is damaged, replace it and update the register.' (2) 'If the card is damaged, replace it. Update the register.'
items.taskText: What does the new sentence boundary most naturally change?
options: It changes replacing the card from a requirement into a suggestion.
It makes updating the register a condition for damaging the card.
It presents updating the register as a separate instruction, rather than clearly sharing the condition.
It changes the register update into a description of a completed action.
items.answer: It presents updating the register as a separate instruction, rather than clearly sharing the condition.
items.explanation: In the first, both actions sit under 'if'; in the second, the update stands as its own command, though context may still connect them.

rationales.It changes replacing the card from a req: Both versions use an imperative for replacement; the full stop does not make it a suggestion.
rationales.It makes updating the register a conditi: Neither wording says updating causes or is required for damage.
rationales.It presents updating the register as a s: In the first, both actions sit under 'if'; in the second, the update stands as its own command, though context may still connect them.
rationales.It changes the register update into a de: 'Update' remains an instruction, not a past-tense report.

findings: Invoice/planning-call repeated the same however punctuation choice without a real contrast.
audit.microSkill: Sentence boundary and scope of a condition over instructions
audit.pedagogicalValue: Shows how splitting coordinated commands can weaken an explicit shared condition.
audit.levelReason: Interprets a practical scope change rather than selecting elementary punctuation.
audit.similarityNote: Meaning comparison of two grammatical versions; acknowledges contextual linkage.

items.setupText: In a factual account, repair 'The coach missed the turning. Causing a twenty-minute delay.' Use one complete sentence.
items.taskText: Which revision connects the result to the missed turning without inventing another cause?

The coach missed the turning, causing a twenty-minute delay.
Causing a twenty-minute delay. The coach missed the turning.
The coach missed the turning because of a twenty-minute delay.
items.answer: The coach missed the turning, causing a twenty-minute delay.
items.explanation: The comma attaches the result phrase to the event it follows and results from.

rationales.The coach missed the turning; causing a: The semicolon still leaves a nonfinite result phrase where an independent clause is expected.
rationales.Causing a twenty-minute delay. The coach: Moving the result fragment does not make it an independent sentence.
rationales.The coach missed the turning, causing a: The comma attaches the result phrase to the event it follows and results from.
rationales.The coach missed the turning because of: This reverses the stated causal relationship: the delay now causes the missed turning.

findings: Lesson-plan/hiring-process provided an unexplained however contrast and formulaic feedback.
audit.microSkill: Attach a supplementary result clause with a comma
audit.pedagogicalValue: Repairs a nonfinite fragment while preserving its causal direction.
audit.levelReason: Combines sentence completeness with result interpretation.
audit.similarityNote: Result supplement, not a purpose phrase or reduced relative.

items.setupText: An editor wants the afterthought inside parentheses within the same sentence.

The replacement pump (it arrived yesterday). Is already leaking.
The replacement pump it arrived (yesterday) is already leaking.
The replacement pump (it arrived yesterday) is already leaking.
items.answer: The replacement pump (it arrived yesterday) is already leaking.

rationales.The replacement pump (it arrived yesterd: The parenthetical sentence is inserted inside the larger sentence; removing it leaves 'The replacement pump is already leaking'.
The parentheses swallow the main predicate and contain an incorrectly joined clause sequence.
The full stop separates the main subject from 'is already leaking'.
rationales.The replacement pump it arrived (yesterd: Bracketing only the time word leaves the parenthetical clause unmarked inside the main clause.

findings: Survey/project-dashboard tail was implausible with students arriving and all messages were repeated.
audit.microSkill: Independent parenthetical clause within a host sentence
audit.pedagogicalValue: Checks both the inserted clause and the surrounding host independently.
audit.levelReason: A finite parenthesis interrupts an extended main subject-predicate connection.
audit.similarityNote: Parenthesis is itself independent, unlike the B1 relative-clause insertion.

items.setupText: The writer means that the funds were insufficient despite a donation. Keep that contrast in one complete sentence.

Despite a large donation, the repairs remained unaffordable.
A large donation, the repairs remained unaffordable.
Because of a large donation, the repairs remained unaffordable.

items.explanation: The comma links the concessive phrase to the main statement while preserving the contrast.

rationales.Despite a large donation; the repairs re: The opening prepositional phrase is not an independent clause, so a semicolon is inappropriate here.
rationales.Despite a large donation, the repairs re: The comma links the concessive phrase to the main statement while preserving the contrast.
rationales.A large donation, the repairs remained u: Removing 'despite' removes the phrase's connection to the main clause.
rationales.Because of a large donation, the repairs: This makes the donation the cause of unaffordability, not something that failed to overcome it.

findings: Manual/board-discussion repeated the same however frame with no item-specific explanation.
audit.microSkill: Boundary after a concessive prepositional phrase
audit.pedagogicalValue: Distinguishes a prepositional adjunct from a complete clause without changing its meaning.
audit.levelReason: Requires both form and concession to survive an edit.

items.setupText: The writer is addressing the trainees, not saying that someone should thank them.
